items.item: The dual-write measurement's two halves share the same table shape, slot plugin and decoding method, differing only in whether the event was written in the order's own transaction or a separate one, isolating the transaction boundary itself as the only variable between loss and recovery.

The routing measurement uses two genuinely different aggregate types (order, shipment) rather than two rows of the same type, so the different-topic outcome demonstrates the router's own aggregatetype-based logic rather than an artifact of two otherwise-identical rows.

The ordering measurement deliberately interleaves the two aggregates' own writes in the insert order itself (A, B, A, B), rather than writing one aggregate's events together and the other's separately, so the correct per-aggregate ordering it recovers cannot be an artifact of how the events happened to be written.

The cleanup measurement captures the insert with one call to the decoding function before the delete is even issued, rather than issuing both writes first and decoding afterward, so the proof demonstrates genuine capture-then-cleanup ordering rather than two writes that merely happened to both appear in one later read.

The wrong option in the first predict question — that the database still knows the publish is owed — is ruled out by the measured mechanism itself: the decoded stream after the crash contains zero outbox inserts, meaning nothing was ever written anywhere that could later be consulted to recover or even notice the missing announcement.

The wrong option in the final predict question — that the router's delete-filtering makes cleanup timing irrelevant — is ruled out directly by the measured cleanup function: filtering protects only against the delete itself leaking through as a fake event, which is a separate concern from whether the row's own insert was captured before it was removed.

The outbox fix in the first function reuses the identical connection pattern as the failing dual-write half (one connection, one transaction, one commit), differing only in whether the outbox INSERT is inside that same transaction, so the recovered event's presence traces specifically to the transaction boundary and not to any other difference in how the two halves connect or commit.

The router's own dedup-key claim is checked against the outbox row's own id column rather than against the aggregateid, since the documentation's own id field is what a consumer is told to use for deduplication, and conflating it with the aggregateid would understate what the row actually carries for that purpose.

Every scratch table and replication slot this topic creates is confirmed dropped inside the same function that created it, verified by three successive clean runs of examples.py, and the shared orders table is never touched by any of this topic's four functions.
